S&P, Nasdaq futures inch up

Early in the session, unconfirmed reports that Qatar and Pakistan had put forward a proposal to revive talks to conclude the Iran war briefly sent oil prices down to $106 a barrel from $112 a barrels. The rumors bolstered sentiment, which has been dented in recent sessions by worries over the sustainability of massive debt-fueled AI infrastructure spending and elevated borrowing costs.

"The relief from energy that played out late in the European session meant equities rallied as investors overcame some of their earlier AI jitters," analysts at Deutsche Bank said in a note.

At 07:47 ET, spot gold had fallen 0.1% to $4,121.13 an ounce, while gold futures had declined 0.1% to $4,138.51 an ounce.

Gold has fallen more than 1% since the start of the week and remains down around a fifth since the Iran conflict erupted in late February, disrupting energy markets and pushing up oil prices. Worries over energy-driven inflation have underpinned bets that the central banks, including the Federal Reserve, may need to tighten monetary policy. Higher borrowing costs present a possible headwind for gold because the yellow metal does not pay interest.

Key Takeaways

Pinterest stock is up 20% in the past month through Monday's close, while the S&P 500 rose less than 1% and Snap gained 13%.

The stock bounced off a September low near the price Pinterest paid to buy back its own shares, and two social-media rallies carried it higher in October.

Even after the run, Pinterest trades at 10x forward earnings, against a five-year average of 24x.

Third-quarter results in early November will be the first with Amazon veteran James Dibbo as CFO, and they need to show US and Canada growth holding near Q2's 18%.

Pinterest (PINS:NYSE) stock is up 20% in the past month (through Monday's close), while the S&P 500 rose 0.6% and the Nasdaq 100 slipped 0.4%. Snap (SNAP:NYSE) gained 13% over the same stretch.

The strange part? Pinterest hasn't put out a new quarterly number since early August.

A September low, then an October run

The month started from a rough spot. Pinterest dropped 9% on Sept. 9 after CEO Bill Ready warned at a Goldman Sachs conference that the international business was under pressure, from new EU limits on Asia-based cross-border sellers and from a reshuffle of how it sells overseas. The slide went on through a 5% drop on Sept. 22, with no news behind it.

But it ran out of steam at an interesting level. Pinterest spent more than $2 billion buying back its own stock this year through early August, at an average price of $18.17, and the shares bottomed in September just above that.

Then October did all the work: the stock climbed 20% from Sept. 30 to Oct. 15. Snap jumped 7% on Oct. 9 as social-media stocks rallied together, and Pinterest rose 4.2%. The group rallied again on Oct. 13, and Pinterest added 4.4%. Two days later it gained another 4.4% as UBS kept its Buy rating and $33 target.

TIKR tracks 39 analysts on Pinterest. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Pinterest, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Pinterest's Analyst Ratings

Amazon's ad money man takes over

The only real company news came on Oct. 5, after the close, when Pinterest named James Dibbo CFO, starting Oct. 26. At Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ), Dibbo ran finance for Amazon Ads and Prime Video, among other businesses. The stock barely reacted, rising about 1% after hours.

I think the hire matters more than that. Ready has been blunt about where Pinterest falls short: "We 5x the number of clicks to advertisers over that last 3-year period, but we certainly didn't 5x the revenue," he said on the second-quarter call.

Key Takeaways

Shopify stock is up 33% in the past month (through Monday's close), and about half of that came in the two sessions after it brought Shop Pay checkout to Meta's Muse AI agent.

Amazon had blocked Muse from its site the day before, and Shopify says an order placed by an AI agent earns it the same as an order on a merchant's own store.

Analyst calls and target raises carried most of the rest, and the stock now trades close to the Street's $176 mean target at about 81x forward earnings.

Third-quarter results come before the open on Nov. 3, and the stock needs a beat that lifts next year's estimates to keep climbing.

Shopify (SHOP:NASDAQ) stock is up 33% in the past month (through Monday's close), while the Nasdaq 100 slipped 0.4%.

And Shopify shareholders have Muse to thank.

The day after Amazon said no

On Sunday, Sept. 20, Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) started blocking Muse, the AI agent from Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ), from shopping its site. The next day, Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke posted on X that Shopify was "partnering deeply with Muse to enable agentic checkout with Shop Pay on all Shopify stores."

Shares jumped 7.3% that Monday and another 7.1% on Tuesday: about half the month's gain in two sessions. A leaked Muse checkout screen listing Meta Pay next to Shop Pay didn't stop the run.

Agents pay full freight

The best part is what Shopify earns on those orders. On the Q2 call, President Harley Finkelstein said agentic transactions "carry the exact economics as an online store transaction."

And there are more of them. In Q2, AI-driven orders to Shopify stores tripled from a year earlier, while gross merchandise volume rose 32% to $116 billion.

The risk is that Meta eventually wants a cut of every sale Muse makes.

Then Wall Street piled on

Shares rose 5.8% on Oct. 5, when Piper Sandler said demand for migrations to Shopify had increased materially (softer jobs data helped, too). They added 4.9% on Oct. 12, as Cantor Fitzgerald raised its target to $158 from $145 and Deutsche Bank said Shopify can win big from agentic commerce over the long run. JPMorgan, Baird and RBC lifted theirs to $190 or $200.

Priced for a strong Nov. 3

Estimates climbed even faster than the stock, so Shopify's forward P/E fell to about 81x, from 95x a year earlier.
